pages.title: Utopia Trip story approval — public-marketing scope
pages.excerpt: Ben confirms (2026-06-01) that community + individual consent exists for the full Utopia trip content (21–22 May 2026) to be used in ACT's public-facing Goods on Country marketing — newsletters, social, the website funnels — not only ACT's closed internal ecosystem. This record is the fresh per-destination approval the Oonchiumpa verbal-consent pattern explicitly requires when a public/newsletter destination appears, and it follows that pattern's governance shape.
pages.content:
> Ben confirms (2026-06-01) that community + individual consent exists for the **full Utopia trip** content (21–22 May 2026) to be used in ACT's **public-facing Goods on Country marketing** — newsletters, social, the website funnels — not only ACT's closed internal ecosystem. This record is the **fresh per-destination approval** the [Oonchiumpa verbal-consent pattern](2026-04-18-oonchiumpa-story-approval.md) explicitly requires when a public/newsletter destination appears, and it follows that pattern's governance shape.

## This specific approval

- **Who:** the communities and individuals featured in the Utopia trip content, via **Oonchiumpa** as cultural authority.
- **Authority holder:** Kristy Bloomfield (Central/Eastern Arrernte, Alyawarra TO of Mparntwe) + Tanya Turner (Eastern Arrernte), Oonchiumpa co-directors.
- **When:** consent given around/through the Utopia trip (May 2026); confirmed and recorded by Ben **2026-06-01**.
- **Consent mode:** verbal-in-conversation, **Ben-as-witness** — the first-class ACT pattern (the witness-record written promptly IS the audit trail; no contract required).
- **Scope (NEW, broader than the April Oonchiumpa approval):** public-facing Goods on Country marketing — **newsletters · social · website funnels** — plus funder decks and internal use.
- **Youth — Mykel:** parent/guardian **and** Oonchiumpa **explicitly cleared** Mykel (a young person) to appear, **named**, as a public campaign face. This satisfies the PICC selective-youth rule (explicit + specific, not blanket).

## Names — verified vs TO-VERIFY (do not publish an unverified name)

- **VERIFIED:** Kristy Bloomfield · Tanya Turner (Oonchiumpa) · Cliff Plummer (Tennant Creek, consented voice) · Mykel (first name; cleared).
- **TO VERIFY before naming publicly — run UN-NAMED until Ben confirms spelling/role:**
  - The two **Ampilatwatja OAM Elders** (2026 Order of Australia recipients) — names were "TBC" in the source.
  - **Frank & Casey Holmes** (Antarrengeny) — confirm spelling.
  - **Dianne Stokes**, **Norman Frank** — confirm spelling/role.
- **Place names to hold to:** Utopia · Ampilatwatja · Antarrengeny · Tennant Creek · Mparntwe. **Oonchiumpa** (never "Ntumba").

## Excluded — NOT covered by this approval

- The **"Linda Turner — Maningrida"** story is **DO-NOT-USE**. Maningrida is a different community, not the Utopia trip — **permanently excluded** from all Goods marketing.
- Any destination beyond Goods public marketing + funder decks (external journalist, book publisher, a third party's channel) needs its **own** per-destination approval.

## Recipient-side consent is a separate axis

Storyteller consent (this record) ≠ recipient opt-in. Newsletter sends still obey [newsletter-consent-policy](newsletter-consent-policy.md): only contacts with `newsletter_consent = true` receive a send (use `v_newsletter_audience`). A tag is a segment, not consent.

## Withdrawal

Any featured individual, or Oonchiumpa on their behalf, can withdraw at any time. Withdrawal **outweighs** this approval and is honoured immediately — the content is pulled, no questions.

---
*Effect: the Utopia-trip content in `thoughts/shared/goods-content-inventory.md` moves from `pending` → `consented` for public-marketing use, EXCEPT (a) the excluded Maningrida story and (b) any specific personal NAME still in the TO-VERIFY list, which runs un-named until confirmed.*

pages.title: Vic
pages.excerpt: The wound becomes wisdom only when someone chooses to turn back and hand the map to the person still lost in it.
pages.content:
> The wound becomes wisdom only when someone chooses to turn back and hand the map to the person still lost in it.

## Who Vic Is

Vic is a person whose story sits at the intersection of addiction recovery and community service — a transformation narrative published through the ACT content platform and documented in ACT's wider sovereign-story ecosystem. The article "A Hero's Journey from Addiction to Inspiration: The Life of Vic" was published on 2025-10-11 and is one of a cluster of transformation stories in the ACT archive.

The specifics of Vic's background — hometown, program, demographic details — are not disclosed in the published source material. What the article traces is an arc rather than a biography: a person who grew up in an environment where addiction was a common response to hardship, who entered a rehabilitation program, and who came out the other side choosing to use their experience to help others.

This is not unusual in ACT's storytelling ecosystem. What makes Vic's story worth documenting is the same thing that makes Joe Kwon's ConFit work and Oonchiumpa's mentors worth documenting: the turn. The moment a person's hardest years become someone else's foothold.

## The Pattern ACT Recognises

ACT returns often to this particular human architecture: someone who has been through the justice system or addiction or homelessness, and who, on the other side, doesn't leave. They stay in proximity. They become the thing they once needed.

Vic's story belongs to this pattern. The published narrative describes the rehabilitation program as providing not just recovery tools but "tools for personal growth and development" — framing the intervention as more than clinical. The decision to then dedicate life to helping others facing similar struggles is framed as an act of agency, not charity: Vic has something others need, and chooses to give it.

This is the same logic that makes Joe Kwon's ConFit work. It is the same logic that makes Oonchiumpa's mentorship model function — adults who stayed. It is what CONTAINED tries to communicate to policymakers: the people inside the system, and those who have come through it, carry intelligence the system itself can't generate.

## Connection to ConFit Pathways

Vic's story is thematically adjacent to ConFit Pathways, though a direct operational connection is not confirmed in available source material.

ConFit Pathways — founded by Joe Kwon, who built his own transformation inside prison and emerged to found a fitness and mentorship program for young people at justice risk — is the clearest structural parallel. Both Vic and Joe Kwon inhabit the same role: the person who doesn't let their hardest experience be only about them.

The Bimberi Youth Justice Centre partnership between ConFit and ReSOLEution runs on this same principle. Evidence for the 60% reduction in recidivism among ConFit participants tracked in [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] rests partly on what a lived-experience mentor can provide that no institutional worker can.

## Connection to JusticeHub

[[justicehub|JusticeHub]] tracks community programs with documented outcomes. The lived-experience mentorship model — Vic's pattern, Joe Kwon's model, the Oonchiumpa approach — appears repeatedly in the evidence base. JusticeHub's research shows community-led programs achieve roughly 78% success rates compared to 15.5% for youth detention. Lived-experience mentors are a structural feature of most programs in the upper tier.

Vic's story, as a published narrative in the ACT ecosystem, feeds the story layer that makes JusticeHub's evidence emotionally legible. The data says community programs work better. Vic's story explains why.

## Connection to Empathy Ledger

Stories like Vic's — recovery narratives with a community service arc — are the type of material the Empathy Ledger platform is built to hold and protect. The platform's consent architecture ensures that storytellers retain sovereignty over how their narrative is used, shared, and cited.

The published article about Vic was sourced from the ACT articles database (Supabase article ID: f566643d-6d12-4f69-88c1-3ab5de02c0dd, published 2025-10-11). It does not identify Vic by surname or disclose identifying details beyond the transformation arc — consistent with the Empathy Ledger principle that protection and publication are not opposites.

## The Arc as Methodology

There is a reason ACT documents this pattern repeatedly, in multiple people's lives.

The LCAA method — Listen, Curiosity, Action, Art — describes how ACT approaches its work. Vic's story follows a parallel arc. Someone listens to a person in crisis. Curiosity opens — about what is possible, what exists, what a different life might look like. Action follows: the rehabilitation program, the choice to re-enter. Art is what comes after: the public testimony, the presence as someone who has been through it and stayed.

The person who survives the system and then helps redesign it is not a side character in ACT's work. It's a central figure. CONTAINED's Isaiah — a young man who helped build the Voices Room, went from surviving the system to working at Interlace Advisory. Joe Kwon, who built ConFit after prison. The Oonchiumpa mentors who stay close when other services create distance. Vic belongs to this same lineage.

What makes these people valuable is not the hardship. It's the turn. The deliberate choice to remain useful to people who are still in the place they came from.

## Evidence Note

The source article "A Hero's Journey from Addiction to Inspiration" (published 2025-10-11, Supabase article ID f566643d-6d12-4f69-88c1-3ab5de02c0dd) is sparse on specifics: no age, location, substance, program name, or date of recovery is given. The wiki has not yet absorbed deeper sources for this profile. What is documented is the arc and its significance to the ACT storytelling ecosystem. If Vic has participated in further programs or has a direct ConFit or JusticeHub connection, that detail should be added when sourced.

## Published Writing

- **"A Hero's Journey from Addiction to Inspiration: The Life of Vic"** (2025-10-11) — transformation narrative documenting Vic's arc from addiction through rehabilitation to community service; published through the ACT content platform.

## Backlinks

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — lived-experience mentorship as core of the evidence base

pages.title: Vignette & Media Workflows
pages.excerpt: How to create, update, and manage story vignettes with media integration from Empathy Ledger.
pages.content:
> How to create, update, and manage story vignettes with media integration from Empathy Ledger.

## Overview

Story vignettes are the compendium's unit of impact evidence — short, structured documents that link a consented community story to [[alma|ALMA]] review fields, project context, and media. They are static markdown files with rich YAML frontmatter, sourced from Empathy Ledger and built into the compendium.

## Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    EMPATHY LEDGER V2                        │
│  stories table, media_items table, media_storytellers       │
│  DB Functions: extract_descript_id(), generate_embed()      │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  MANUAL/SYNC PROCESS                        │
│  1. Query EL for stories with project_slugs                 │
│  2. Check consent status (only process if granted)          │
│  3. Extract Descript video IDs                              │
│  4. Update vignette YAML frontmatter                        │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   COMPENDIUM (STATIC)                       │
│  Markdown files with YAML frontmatter                       │
│  Descript iframes (conditional on consent_scope)            │
│  Photo URLs (Supabase storage)                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Workflow 1: Creating a New Vignette

### Prerequisites
- Story exists in Empathy Ledger with proper consent
- ALMA review fields have been assessed (see [[transcription-workflow|Transcription Workflow]])
- Cultural review status is known
- Media assets are uploaded (if applicable)

### Steps

1. **Check Empathy Ledger record** — verify consent is granted, note the `empathy_ledger_id` UUID, review linked media
2. **Copy vignette template** to the appropriate category folder: `[number]-[slug].md`
3. **Update frontmatter:**
   - Set `title`, `slug`, `vignette_number`, `category`
   - Link `empathy_ledger_id`
   - Set `consent_scope` (INTERNAL / EXTERNAL-LITE / EXTERNAL)
   - Set `cultural_review_status` and related fields
   - Add `project_slugs` array
   - Set `place_country`, `voice_owner`, `voice_role`
   - Complete the six legacy `alma_signals` review fields (1-5)
   - Set `lcaa_stage` and `lcaa_shift`
   - Add media references if available
4. **Write content** — opening quote, story summary, ALMA reflection, cultural notes, provenance
5. **Update index** — add to `vignettes/index.md` in appropriate category table

## Workflow 2: Adding Media

### Adding a Descript Video

1. Get Descript share URL: `https://share.descript.com/view/{VIDEO_ID}`
2. Extract video ID (last segment of URL)
3. Update frontmatter:
   ```yaml
   media:
     descript_video_id: "7IJdp8r9FgE"
     descript_url: "https://share.descript.com/view/7IJdp8r9FgE"
   ```
4. Add iframe embed in content (for EXTERNAL-LITE or EXTERNAL consent only):
   ```html
   <iframe
     src="https://share.descript.com/embed/7IJdp8r9FgE"
     width="100%" height="400" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen>
   </iframe>
   ```

### Adding Photos

1. Upload to Empathy Ledger Media Library with full metadata, set consent_status to granted
2. Get Supabase storage URL
3. Update frontmatter:
   ```yaml
   media:
     photos:
       - id: "el-media-uuid-1"
         url: "https://your-project.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/media/path/photo.jpg"
         alt: "Description of photo"
         consent_status: "granted"
   ```

## Workflow 3: Updating ALMA Review Fields

Update when: after community story review, when new evidence emerges, during periodic compendium audits.

```yaml
alma_signals:
  evidence_strength: 4       # 1-5
  community_authority: 5     # 1-5
  harm_risk_inverted: 3      # 1-5 (5 = lowest risk)
  implementation_capability: 4
  option_value: 4
  community_value_return: 5
  overall_score: 4.2         # Average
```

## Workflow 4: Managing Consent Status

| Scope | Meaning | Media Behavior |
|-------|---------|----------------|
| **INTERNAL** | Team only | Video/photos show placeholder |
| **EXTERNAL-LITE** | Shareable with review | May need cultural review |
| **EXTERNAL** | Fully cleared | Full media access |

### Changing Consent Status

1. Update in Empathy Ledger first (source of truth)
2. Update vignette frontmatter to match
3. Add or remove embeds/images accordingly
4. Move in consent scope index table

### If Consent is Withdrawn

1. Immediately set `consent_scope: "INTERNAL"` in vignette
2. Update Empathy Ledger record
3. Remove all embeds, replace with placeholders
4. Remove identifying details from content
5. Consider archiving the vignette entirely

## Workflow 5: Cultural Review

**When required:** All Palm Island content, First Nations youth stories, stories involving sacred sites or ceremonies, stories with `cultural_sensitivity_level: sensitive` or higher.

**Who reviews:** For Palm Island — PICC Elders Council. For Oonchiumpa — relevant cultural advisors. For other projects — project-specific Elders.

**Process:** Prepare draft (not full compendium), share proposed media, note intended use. Conduct review in-person where possible for sensitive content. Document outcome in frontmatter.

## Workflow 6: Bidirectional Project Linking

```yaml
# In vignette frontmatter
project_slugs:
  - oonchiumpa
  - justicehub
  - empathy-ledger

# In project page
linked_vignettes:
  - 15-m-homelessness-independent
  - 16-community-recognition-referrals
```

After linking, recalculate project-level ALMA review summaries only for internal review. Do not present them as a community ranking.

## File Naming Conventions

```
vignettes/[category]/[number]-[slug].md
```

Category folders: `platform-methodology/`, `palm-island/`, `justice-youth/`, `oonchiumpa/`, `system-outcomes/`

## Verification Checklist

Before publishing a new or updated vignette:

- [ ] Consent verified in Empathy Ledger
- [ ] Cultural review completed (if required)
- [ ] ALMA review fields completed (all 6)
- [ ] All frontmatter fields populated
- [ ] Content respects consent scope
- [ ] Media embeds appropriate for scope
- [ ] Index updated
- [ ] Project page(s) updated
- [ ] Cross-links working

## URL Reference

| Source | Pattern |
|--------|---------|
| Descript view | `https://share.descript.com/view/{VIDEO_ID}` |
| Descript embed | `https://share.descript.com/embed/{VIDEO_ID}` |
| Supabase storage | `https://{PROJECT}.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/{BUCKET}/{PATH}` |

pages.title: Ways of Working
pages.excerpt: Our way of working is part of the output. How we show up is the first signal of trust.
pages.content:
> Our way of working is part of the output. How we show up is the first signal of trust.

## Overview

ACT's internal working practices aren't administrative procedures — they're expressions of values. The process is the product. If the way we work isn't respectful, the outcomes won't be either. This article documents the daily rhythms, meeting practices, media governance, and decision-making principles that keep the team aligned.

## Daily Practice

| Practice | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| **Listen first** | If in doubt, pause and return to community voice |
| **Use LCAA** | Structure planning and delivery through the phases |
| **Use ALMA** | Check consent, authority, provenance, review, and action readiness |
| **Ground language** | Keep it non-extractive, honest, no savior framing |
| **Mark nuance** | Tag high-nuance partner details as `[INTERNAL ONLY]` |

## ACT Voice in Daily Work

When writing and communicating, hold these qualities:

| Quality | What It Means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Warm** | Approachable, human, inviting |
| **Grounded** | Based in practice, not theory |
| **Humble** | We don't have all the answers |
| **Visionary** | We see what's possible |
| **Professional yet rebellious** | Serious about the work, questioning the system |

**Do:** Use regenerative metaphors with restraint, ground claims in lived practice, acknowledge uncertainty, center community voice.

**Don't:** Corporate jargon, savior framing, overclaiming, speaking for communities.

See [[voice-guide|ACT Voice Guide]] for the full language system.

## Recurring Calls to Action

Small, repeatable actions that keep the model real:

1. Apply the [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] framework to every project plan and update
2. Route listening-to-action decisions through Empathy Ledger and [[alma|ALMA]]
3. Keep enterprise pathways practical and community-led (The Harvest, Goods on Country)
4. Protect consent and cultural protocols at every stage
5. Review claims before external sharing

> If a call to action cannot be done this week, it is not a call to action.

## Meeting Practice

### Before
- Clear purpose documented
- Right people invited
- Materials shared in advance

### During
- Listen before speaking
- Note who holds authority
- Capture next actions clearly

### After
- Actions distributed within 24 hours
- Consent confirmed where needed
- LCAA phase noted

## Knowledge Capture

Weekly rhythms:
- Update the agent system with project slugs, consent status, authority, provenance, and review fields
- Capture learnings in the appropriate space (Telegram or Discord)
- Review shareability before any external communication
- Run the [[social-soil-canvas|Social Soil Canvas]] when the field feels noisy — especially before adding work, after a hard week, or before making a portfolio cut
- Keep the public website aligned to upstream truth using the [[living-website-operating-system|Living Website Operating System]] — wiki first for durable framing, EL for live story/media, website for composition

## Field Diagnostics

When projects multiply faster than proof, stop planning and diagnose the field.

The [[social-soil-canvas|Social Soil Canvas]] is the founder-facing diagnostic for this. It looks at what is visible above ground (projects, people, rhythms, product packaging) and what sits beneath it (friction, learning, root-system health). The point is not introspection for its own sake. The point is to produce one decision, one pattern, and one proof line that improve the field this week.

## Media Governance

Empathy Ledger is the source of truth for stories, photos, video, and consent records.

Before using any media:
1. Check consent status
2. Verify current (not expired)
3. Confirm appropriate scope
4. Attribute properly

## Data Hygiene

Every record should have:
- Clear ownership
- Version tracking
- Consent flags
- Review date

## Infrastructure Philosophy

> "If a system is loud, it is not doing its job. Quiet systems create room for people to show up."

- Fewer tools, clearer pathways
- Faster handover
- Quiet reliability
- Infrastructure serves the work, not the other way around

See [[act-architecture|ACT Technical Architecture]] for how this applies to systems.

## Conflict Navigation

When principles seem to conflict, prioritize in this order:

1. **Country sets the pace** — Land and community readiness come first
2. **Community authority comes first** — Their voice, their decision
3. **Share with care** — If uncertain, keep internal

## Process Is Product

How we work reflects what we believe. Every interaction is an expression of values. There is no "once we scale, we'll do it properly" — the way we work now is the standard.

pages.title: What are ACT's seven flagship experiences and how does each one convert into ecosystem growth?
pages.excerpt: Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.
pages.content:
> Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.

## Answer

## Seven Experiences That Grow the Ecosystem

ACT doesn't market. It makes things people can't unsee. Each flagship experience serves a different audience, creates a different emotional response, and feeds a different part of the ecosystem. Together they form a complete growth engine that runs on word of mouth.

### 1. CONTAINED — the room that changes politicians

**What it is:** A shipping container retrofitted to simulate what youth detention feels like. 30 minutes. Three rooms. You stand where a child stands.

**Who it's for:** Politicians, public servants, funders, media, general public.

**The emotional move:** Moral shock. You walk in thinking you understand youth justice. You walk out knowing you didn't.

**What it feeds:**
- Media coverage (every journalist who enters writes about it)
- Political will (a minister who's been inside can't vote the same way)
- Touring revenue (venue partnerships, festival activations)
- The Brave Ones (portraits live inside the container's walls)
- Narrative claims (strongest confrontational-frame material)

### 2. Judges on Country — the decision that haunts

**What it is:** 30 minutes on Country in Mparntwe. Traditional Owners hand judges a photo and say: decide. Then reveal what they didn't know.

**Who it's for:** Judges, magistrates, judicial educators, law students.

**The emotional move:** Professional uncertainty. They realise they've been deciding without knowing who the person is.

**What it feeds:**
- Judicial referral patterns (more diversion, more community-based options)
- JusticeHub adoption (every judge with a bookmarked search is a user)
- Word of mouth along the bench (judges talk to judges)
- R&D evidence (novel judicial education methodology)
- Narrative claims (moral-frame material for grants and media)

### 3. The Brave Ones — the portrait you stand in front of

**What it is:** Studio-quality B&W portraits of young people who walked out the other side. Counter-mugshot. Dignity register. Life-size prints.

**Who it's for:** Gallery visitors, arts funders, cultural institutions, the general public.

**The emotional move:** Recognition. You see a person, not a statistic. The portrait demands you stay.

**What it feeds:**
- Gallery touring revenue (MCA, NGV, Powerhouse, parliament foyers)
- Arts funding pipeline (Australia Council, Creative Australia, philanthropic trusts)
- Empathy Ledger growth (every portrait = new storyteller, new consent, new story)
- Brave Ones book (Year 3 — publishable IP)
- Lead-funder naming opportunity ("The [Funder] Brave Ones Portrait Series")

### 4. The Harvest — the meal that grounds everything

**What it is:** Community meals at the farm in Witta. Food from the ground you're standing on. Shared tables. No PowerPoint.

**Who it's for:** Local community, neighbours, potential supporters, partner organisations.

**The emotional move:** Belonging. You eat together. You hear a story. You realise this isn't an organisation — it's a place.

**What it feeds:**
- CSA subscriptions and produce revenue
- Farm-gate event income
- Community trust (the neighbours become advocates)
- Empathy Ledger stories (meal conversations become narratives)
- R&D evidence for The Harvest and Farm projects

### 5. Goods on Country — the box that arrives

**What it is:** Physical products made by communities. Each box comes with a story from Empathy Ledger. You know the person who made what you're holding.

**Who it's for:** Conscious consumers, corporate gift buyers, partner organisations.

**The emotional move:** Connection. This isn't a product. It's a relationship with a place and a person.

**What it feeds:**
- Direct product revenue
- Supply chain data (IoT telemetry, marketplace development — R&D eligible)
- Community enterprise income (revenue flows to producers)
- Empathy Ledger stories (every producer is a storyteller)
- Corporate partnerships (branded Goods boxes as staff gifts)

### 6. Empathy Ledger stories — the voice you can't unhear

**What it is:** Real stories told by real people with real consent. Published on EL, syndicated to JusticeHub. Not marketing. Not case studies. Sovereign narratives.

**Who it's for:** Anyone who finds them — funders, researchers, journalists, community members, other organisations.

**The emotional move:** Intimacy. Laquisha saying "Oppression." Nigel saying "I'm panicking." These aren't pull quotes. They're diagnoses.

**What it feeds:**
- Grant evidence (the strongest material in any application)
- Media coverage (journalists quote real voices, not spokespeople)
- Platform proof (EL working at scale with consent = licensable)
- Narrative claims (every story is multiple claims)
- Academic citations (researchers reference EL stories)

### 7. Tractorpedia — the depth that earns trust

**What it is:** 205 articles of genuine knowledge. Searchable. Linked. Every claim sourced. Every project documented.

**Who it's for:** Funders doing due diligence, researchers, potential partners, other organisations, journalists.

**The emotional move:** Respect. "How does a small organisation know this much?" Trust through depth.

**What it feeds:**
- Grant success rate (the wiki IS the application backing)
- SEO and findability (funders google, wiki appears)
- Partnership credibility (organisations see the depth and want to collaborate)
- Platform licensing proof (the knowledge base demonstrates domain expertise)
- Internal clarity (the team knows what it knows)

### How they compound together

\`\`\`
CONTAINED → judge is moved → attends Judges on Country → sees Brave Ones portrait
→ scans QR → finds JusticeHub → reads EL story → shares with colleagues
→ colleague googles ACT → finds Tractorpedia → reads 205 articles
→ contacts ACT → receives Goods on Country box → attends Harvest meal
→ becomes champion → introduces funder → funder reads wiki → funds next round
\`\`\`

No single experience does everything. But each one creates a thread that pulls toward the next. The ecosystem grows not because ACT asks people to engage — but because each experience naturally leads to the next one.

### Revenue attribution by experience

| Experience | Revenue type | Estimated annual |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|
| CONTAINED | Venue partnerships, touring, activations | Variable |
| Judges on Country | R&D offset on development, grant evidence | Feeds \$109K offset |
| Brave Ones | Gallery revenue, arts grants, book sales (Y3) | Future |
| The Harvest | CSA, produce, farm-gate events | Growing |
| Goods on Country | Product sales, corporate gifts | Growing |
| EL stories | Grant success rate improvement | Indirect but significant |
| Tractorpedia | Grant backing, partnership conversion | Indirect but significant |

The direct revenue experiences (Harvest, Goods) are small today. The indirect ones (wiki backing grants, EL stories strengthening applications, Judges on Country earning the R&D offset) are already producing \$109K/year. The trajectory is toward \$200K through compound growth across all seven.

## Answer

## Twelve-Month Opportunity Map

The Third Reality framework is built. The platforms exist. The question is: where does it meet the world in the next 12 months?

### Tier 1 — Already in motion (convert within 3 months)

#### 1. Judges on Country → National Judicial Education
**Status:** 55 judges just went through it. Postcards designed. QR to JusticeHub working.
**Next move:** Formal proposal to the National Judicial College of Australia (NJCA) to integrate the card deck + experience into their standard professional development. Also approach state judicial commissions (NSW, VIC, QLD first — largest bench populations).
**Revenue:** \$50-100K per engagement. R&D offset on development.
**Third Reality in action:** Postcard (Voice) + JusticeHub search (Evidence) + CivicGraph gap data (Data).

#### 2. Empathy Ledger Y1 Bespoke Customers
**Status:** PICC, JCF, The Buttery, SMART Recovery — four orgs, \$50K each, \$200K total.
**Next move:** Formalise annual engagement agreements. Invoice on schedule. Document the bespoke work as R&D evidence.
**Revenue:** \$200K recurring from Y1. Foundation for productised EL in Y2.
**Third Reality in action:** Each customer deploys all three layers in their context. PICC uses EL (Voice) + community data (Evidence) + government reporting (Data) to produce annual reports that funders can't ignore.

#### 3. R&D Tax Offset — FY26 Claim
**Status:** \$251K eligible spend tracked. \$109K potential offset. Both founders need to invoice retroactively (\$100K each).
**Next move:** CPA appointment within 2 weeks. Founder invoices by end of April. AusIndustry registration.
**Revenue:** \~\$87K refund (combined founder R&D allocation). Recurring annually.
**Third Reality in action:** The spending intelligence system tags every dollar to a project code, which maps to R&D eligibility. The system IS the evidence.

### Tier 2 — Ready to pitch (convert within 6 months)

#### 4. Minderoo Foundation — Three Circles / STAY
**Status:** Pitch package exists (wiki/projects/justicehub/three-circles.md). \$2.9M / 3 years. 10 anchor communities.
**Next move:** Warm introduction via someone who's been through CONTAINED or Judges on Country. The experience is the pitch — not the deck.
**Revenue:** \$850K H2 Y1, \$1.14M Y2-3.
**Third Reality in action:** The entire Three Circles program IS the Third Reality deployed at national scale. CivicGraph (data spine) + Living Map (evidence) + Empathy Ledger (stories) + STAY journals (art) = the library that ends the program.

#### 5. CivicGraph SaaS — First Commercial Customers
**Status:** \$79-\$1999/mo Stripe tiers. 587K entities. 21 data sources.
**Next move:** Target justice sector intermediaries: law firms doing pro bono, philanthropic advisors, state government policy teams. The pitch: "You're making decisions with partial information. We have the full picture."
**Revenue:** \$400K MRR target Y1.
**Third Reality in action:** CivicGraph IS the systemic data layer. Customers pay for the data. Communities benefit from what the data reveals.

#### 6. Australia Council — Brave Ones Portraits
**Status:** Phase 0 (placeholder). Experience design complete. Pilot budget \~\$15K.
**Next move:** Apply for Creative Australia project funding. Position as "the counter-mugshot archive" — a national photographic project that redefines how Indigenous young people are seen.
**Revenue:** \$80K Phase 2 (25 portraits + first gallery show).
**Third Reality in action:** Each portrait is simultaneously art (Voice), evidence (a young person's documented journey via EL), and data (a new ALMA node in the justice evidence base).

### Tier 3 — Build toward (convert within 12 months)

#### 7. State Justice Department Commissioning Intelligence
**Status:** CivicGraph has the gap data. JusticeHub has the program evidence. No state government has been pitched.
**Next move:** Produce a sample gap analysis for one state (QLD — best data coverage). Show: "Here's where you have no funded alternatives to detention. Here's what exists in neighbouring regions. Here's what it would cost vs detention."
**Revenue:** Government consulting at \$150-300K per engagement.
**Third Reality in action:** Gap analysis (Data) + program evidence (Evidence) + community stories from those regions (Voice) = a commissioning recommendation no bureaucrat could produce alone.

#### 8. International — UK or NZ Pilot
**Status:** CivicGraph UK market entry research exists (wiki/research/civicgraph-uk-market-entry.md). Diagrama partnership in Spain. The pattern is not Australia-specific.
**Next move:** UK has comparable public data infrastructure (Companies House, Charity Commission, government contracts). Build a proof-of-concept UK CivicGraph instance. Approach UK justice reinvestment orgs.
**Revenue:** International SaaS + consulting.
**Third Reality in action:** Same three layers, different jurisdiction. Proves the framework travels.

#### 9. University Research Partnership
**Status:** No formal partnership. ANU law students already work with Oonchiumpa (Kristy's bridge program).
**Next move:** Approach ANU, UNSW, or Melbourne with: "We have 587K linked civic entities, 226 consent-governed storytellers, and 1,775 verified community models. No university has access to this. Let's write papers together."
**Revenue:** ARC funding, PhD candidates (free labour), credibility.
**Third Reality in action:** Academic rigour validates the framework. Publications make it citable. The university gets data access. ACT gets legitimacy.

#### 10. Media Feature — Tractorpedia as Story
**Status:** 206 articles, 17 synthesis pieces, clean health. The wiki is extraordinary for an org this size.
**Next move:** Pitch to The Saturday Paper, Guardian Australia, or ABC: "A two-person organisation in the Sunshine Coast hinterland built the most comprehensive civic intelligence platform in Australia. Here's how."
**Revenue:** None directly. But media coverage converts to funder attention, partner interest, and storyteller trust.
**Third Reality in action:** The story of ACT IS a Third Reality story — systemic data about the justice system + sovereign narratives from communities + evidence that alternatives work, all held in one ecosystem.

### The filter for every opportunity

Before pursuing any of these, ask:

1. **Does it produce Third Reality output?** (Data + Evidence + Voice)
2. **Does it create an experience people will tell others about?**
3. **Does it compound?** (Each round makes the next one better)
4. **Is the R&D eligible?** (43.5% back on development)
5. **Does it move toward Beautiful Obsolescence?** (Can communities run it without ACT eventually?)

If all five: pursue aggressively.
If four: pursue.
If three or fewer: probably admin dressed up as opportunity.

## Answer

## Four Wiki Surfaces

The Tractorpedia wiki feeds four downstream surfaces, each serving a different purpose:

### 1. ACT Regenerative Studio — the public front door
- **URL:** act-regenerative-studio.vercel.app (will become act.place)
- **329 pages** across 13 sections including Sources (150)
- Card-based browser with section tabs, filtering, search
- Receives content via cross-repo GitHub Action dispatch (wiki-content-updated event)
- Includes source summaries, which Tractorpedia excludes
- **Audience:** funders, partners, public, anyone exploring ACT

### 2. Tractorpedia HTML Viewer — the encyclopedia
- **URL:** /tractorpedia.html on Command Center domain
- **189 articles** baked into a single 1.4MB self-contained HTML file
- Wikipedia Vector skin: fixed sidebar, collapsible categories, client-side search with autocomplete
- Built by wiki-build-viewer.mjs, committed by CI
- Fully offline-capable
- **Audience:** deep reading, research, reference

### 3. Command Center /wiki — the ops cockpit
- **URL:** /wiki on Command Center domain
- **189 articles** loaded live from filesystem (snapshot fallback)
- Dark glass UI, homepage is a maintenance dashboard showing repair queue: broken links, orphans, stubs, missing backlinks
- Full-text search, ReactMarkdown renderer, wikilink routing
- Reads status from wiki/output/status-latest.json
- **Audience:** Ben — internal operational use

### 4. Command Center Snapshot — legacy fallback
- 57 markdown files in apps/command-center/public/wiki/
- Labeled "Legacy mirror for command-center compatibility only"
- Only consumed as API fallback when canonical path not found
- Vestigial — canonical wiki/ now covers all paths

### Key Differences

| Surface | Articles | Source Summaries | Search | Audience |
|---------|----------|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Regen Studio | 329 | Yes (150) | Section filter | Public |
| Tractorpedia | 189 | No | Autocomplete | Deep readers |
| Command Center | 189 | No | Full-text | Internal ops |
| Snapshot | 57 | No | None | Legacy fallback |

### Sync Pipeline

Push to main triggers wiki-rebuild.yml:
1. Lint wiki
2. Update search index (OpenAI embeddings if key available)
3. Rebuild viewer + snapshot
4. Copy viewer to public/tractorpedia.html
5. Commit artifacts
6. Dispatch wiki-content-updated to act-regenerative-studio

The current act.place is a temporary holding site. When the Regen Studio moves to act.place, the 329-page wiki becomes the public knowledge layer.

pages.title: What is the living organism — the visual system for The Aesthetics of Asymmetry?
pages.excerpt: Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.
pages.content:
> Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.

## Answer

## The Living Organism: CivicGraph as Art

### What it is

Not a dashboard. Not an analytics platform. A living data organism that breathes, drifts, clusters, and reveals. An artwork made from 587,000 Australian civic entities and the 1.5 million relationships between them, rendered as something you can stand inside, explore, print on a wall, or hold in your hand.

The organism has three states:

**The Network** — the full entity graph. Charities, foundations, government bodies, companies, political donors, procurement recipients. Connected by money, governance, geography, and power. Rendered as a force-directed galaxy where related entities drift together and clusters form organically — not sorted into neat categories but finding their own gravity.

**The Map** — 873 funding deserts. Dark voids where disadvantage is high and funding is low. Not a choropleth with traffic-light colours but an inversion: the deserts are the subject. Funded areas glow. Deserts are absence. The viewer sees what isn't there.

**The Flow** — money in motion. Contracts flowing from government to recipients. Donations flowing from donors to parties. Grants flowing from foundations to communities. Hansard promises floating above, connected to purchase orders (or not) below. The gap between a press release and a funded program, animated.

### The tech stack

**Scale problem:** 587K entities and 1.5M edges. Most JS graph libraries cap at 10-50K. The answer is GPU-accelerated rendering.

| Layer | Tool | Why |
|-------|------|-----|
| Graph engine | Graphology | Graph operations, community detection, centrality metrics. Pre-compute server-side. |
| Full network renderer | Cosmos.gl | GPU-powered force layout. Demonstrated at 1M+ nodes in-browser. The only library that genuinely handles ACT's scale. |
| Curated sub-views | Sigma.js v3 | WebGL renderer, mature plugin ecosystem. For focused views of 10-50K node subgraphs (justice sector, foundation network, etc.) |
| Geographic layer | deck.gl + Mapbox GL JS | Funding deserts, contract flows by location, dot-density maps. GPU-powered, handles millions of points. |
| Narrative / scrollytelling | Svelte + Scrollama + D3 | 6-episode story. Each episode triggers transitions on a sticky vis. Proven in data journalism. |
| Organic / generative layer | p5.js | Perlin noise for breathing motion. Boids algorithm for organic clustering. The \"always slightly wrong\" principle — imperfection reads as alive. |
| Data aesthetics (Ikeda style) | Three.js + GLSL shaders | Custom fragment shaders for light grids, scan lines, particle fields. Full control over the visual language. |
| Physical output | p5-svg → AxiDraw plotter | Genuine pen-drawn artifacts from data. SVG export for large-format prints. Risograph colour separation. |
| AI style transfer | ControlNet img2img | Programmatic render as control input, Lombardi/hand-drawn style applied as post-processing. AI adds texture, never invents data. |

### What already exists in GrantScope

GrantScope already has:
- **react-force-graph-2d/3d** — force-directed graphs at /graph, /power, /entity/[id]
- **Leaflet + react-leaflet** — funding desert maps at /map, /places, /power
- **Recharts** — bar/line charts across 8+ report pages
- **Custom Canvas force simulation** — hand-rolled physics at /power/network-graph
- **Pre-computed materialized views** ready for vis:
  - \`mv_funding_deserts\` — desert score by LGA
  - \`mv_board_power\` — board interlock scores
  - \`mv_gs_entity_stats\` — degree centrality, dollar flows
  - \`mv_revolving_door\` — government-to-sector cycling
  - \`mv_youth_justice_entities\` — justice system cross-map

### The 6 episodes as visual installations

Each episode from The Aesthetics of Asymmetry has a specific visual treatment:

**Episode 1: The Keyhole**
A split view. On the left: what a community org sees when applying for a grant (a form, a deadline, a word limit). On the right: the full Cosmos.gl graph showing every entity in their sector, every competing applicant, every funder's portfolio. The keyhole is literal — a circular mask that constrains one side. Scroll to widen the aperture.

**Episode 2: Resolution**
Start with the full graph at maximum blur (Gaussian shader). As you scroll, resolution increases. Names appear. Amounts sharpen. At full resolution, it becomes uncomfortable — you can see individual donation-to-contract chains. The viewer chooses how deep to look. Steyerl's resolution politics, made interactive.

**Episode 3: The Missing Folder**
The map of 873 funding deserts — but rendered as absence. The funded areas are warm particle clouds. The deserts are black. Scroll triggers reveal what is NOT collected: care labour, kinship networks, informal economy, cultural governance. Each absence appears as a label in the void, like Onuoha's empty folders.

**Episode 4: The Promise and the Purchase Order**
Hansard quotes float at the top of the screen. As you scroll, money flows (or doesn't) connect downward to actual funded programs. Where a promise produced a purchase order, a line connects. Where it didn't, the quote drifts and fades. The gap between rhetoric and reality, animated.

**Episode 5: The Alibi**
Flood the screen with data. Everything at once. Every entity, every relationship, every dollar. The Elahi inversion — if you demand transparency, here is all of it. The viewer drowns. Then: a filter appears. Choose a postcode. Choose a sector. The organism contracts to show only what matters to you. From chaos to clarity — but you had to ask for it.

**Episode 6: CARE**
The final episode inverts the gaze. Instead of \"what does the system look like?\" — \"who owns the story?\" Empathy Ledger storytellers appear as points of light within the network. Their stories are the only nodes with voice (audio playback). The surrounding data is context, not subject. The sovereign narrative is the centre. OCAP principles rendered as architecture.

### Making it feel alive

The organism breathes through:
- **Perlin noise displacement** on node positions — everything gently drifts, nothing is pinned
- **Variable opacity based on data freshness** — recently updated entities are brighter, stale ones fade
- **Organic clustering via boids algorithm** — entities that share attributes flock together without rigid categories
- **Time-based colour temperature** — entities shift warm-to-cool based on when their data was last refreshed
- **Heartbeat pulse** on entities with active Empathy Ledger stories — a subtle throb that draws the eye

### Physical artifacts

Every episode produces a printable artifact:
- Episode 1: A literal keyhole-shaped poster. Full graph visible through the hole.
- Episode 2: A gradient print from blur to sharp. Plotter-drawn at AxiDraw resolution.
- Episode 3: A set of empty folders (Onuoha tribute) labelled with what's missing.
- Episode 4: A two-column broadsheet. Left: Hansard quotes. Right: funded (or unfunded) programs.
- Episode 5: A fold-out poster. Closed: chaos. Open: your local data.
- Episode 6: A postcard with a QR code. Scan to hear a storyteller.

### The image generation pipeline

For exhibition-quality pieces:
1. Generate accurate network/map/flow programmatically (Cosmos, Sigma, deck.gl)
2. Export as high-res PNG or SVG
3. Feed through ControlNet with Canny edge detection as control input
4. Prompt: \"hand-drawn investigation board, string and pin, paper texture, Lombardi narrative structure\"
5. The AI adds aesthetic texture while preserving the real data topology
6. Print at exhibition scale (A0+)

Gemini 2.5 with code execution can also generate p5.js sketches from data descriptions — useful for rapid prototyping of generative treatments before committing to full production.

### What this is really about

The organism is not a tool for analysing data. It is an artwork that happens to be made from real data. The difference matters.

A tool says: here is what the data shows.
An artwork says: here is what it feels like to see it.

The 873 funding deserts are not interesting because the number is 873. They are interesting because 873 communities wake up every morning in a system designed to be invisible to them. The organism makes the system visible — not as a dashboard, but as a felt experience.

That is the Third Reality rendered as art. Systemic data + narrative sovereignty = a shared truth you stand inside and can't unsee.

## Answer

## The Narrative Store

The narrative store at \`wiki/narrative/\` is a structured claims database that tracks what ACT has said publicly, where, with what evidence, and how it landed. It turns editorial from a blank-page problem into an assembly problem.

### Structure

\`\`\`
wiki/narrative/
  justicehub/
    INDEX.md                    — all claims, channels, evidence scores
    STRATEGY-REVIEW.md          — what is landing, what is not, where to push
    claim-tier-pricing-against-detention-cost.md
    claim-three-circles-start-at-the-edge.md
    claim-staying-is-the-move.md
    claim-fire-crescendo-build-slowly.md
    claim-authority-at-the-edge-lineage.md
    claim-the-library-is-the-destination.md
    claim-ten-anchor-communities-filter-is-relationship.md
  goods-on-country/
    INDEX.md
    STRATEGY-REVIEW.md
    claim-bed-to-courtroom.md
  empathy-ledger/
    claim-the-tour-is-a-working-tour.md
  sources.json              — external content sources to monitor
  funders.json              — funder profiles with resonance mapping
\`\`\`

### What a Claim File Contains

Each claim file documents:
- **The claim itself** — a specific argument or stat (e.g. "it costs $1,500/night to detain a young person vs $150/night for community-based support")
- **Evidence** — which wiki articles, EL stories, data sources back it up, with strength rating
- **Channel history** — where this claim has been published (LinkedIn, grant application, pitch deck, op-ed)
- **Deployment dates** — when it was used, preventing over-repetition
- **Resonance notes** — what response it got, from whom

### How It Drives Editorial

**Without the narrative store:** Ben opens LinkedIn, stares at blank page, tries to remember what to write about.

**With the narrative store:**
1. \`/wiki narrative status justicehub\` — see all 7 claims, which channels they have been deployed to, evidence strength
2. \`/wiki narrative draft justicehub --frame moral --channel linkedin\` — AI assembles a draft from the strongest unused claims for that channel
3. Ben edits for voice, publishes
4. \`/wiki narrative log "tier-pricing beats detention costs" linkedin\` — claim is marked as deployed on that channel

**For grant applications:**
1. \`/wiki narrative funder minderoo\` — pulls funder profile, cross-references against ACT's claims
2. Assembles a pitch brief showing which claims match funder priorities
3. Evidence links point back to wiki articles and EL stories for the full backing

**For strategy review:**
1. \`/wiki narrative review justicehub\` — weekly editorial retro
2. Which claims are landing? Which channels are working?
3. Where are the gaps? What should we say next?

### Ingestion Pipeline

New claims enter through:
- \`scripts/narrative-ingest.mjs <path>\` — extracts claims from essays, pitches, posts
- \`scripts/narrative-refresh.mjs\` — regenerates INDEX files from claim files
- \`scripts/narrative-strategy-review.mjs\` — generates STRATEGY-REVIEW from deployment history

### The Compounding Effect

Over time, the narrative store becomes a strategic asset:
- Every claim is tested and scored across channels
- Funder profiles accumulate resonance data
- The AI gets better at assembling drafts because the claims library is richer
- Grant applications take hours instead of days because the evidence is pre-linked
- No claim is ever made without traceable backing — critical for credibility

pages.title: What is the Third Reality actually solving and how do CivicGraph, JusticeHub, and Empathy Ledger work together to do it?
pages.excerpt: Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.
pages.content:
> Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-13. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.

## Answer

## What the Third Reality Is Actually Solving

### The broken room

Youth justice in Australia has more reports, more frameworks, more evaluations, more peak bodies, more lived-experience panels, and more government strategies than at any point in history.

It also has more children in detention, more recidivism, and more lateral violence in the sector than at any point in recent memory.

80%+ reoffending. \$1.3M per child per year to produce that failure rate. 60%+ of detained young people are Indigenous.

The problem is not absence of evidence. The problem is that the evidence, the relationships, and the stories are held in different rooms — and the rooms don't talk to each other.

- Frameworks live in consultancy decks
- Stories live in unfunded community organisations
- Funding flows live in spreadsheets nobody reads
- Indigenous knowledge lives where it has always lived — in Country, in Elders, in Tuesday afternoon check-ins that no funder has ever counted as governance

### What the Third Reality says

A spreadsheet of justice statistics alone won't change a policymaker's mind. A singular tragic story can be dismissed as an anomaly. But when you connect an immutable, sovereign human story to verified systemic data, you create something that cannot be ignored.

**Systemic Data + Narrative Sovereignty = The Third Reality**

It is not your story. It is not my story. It is a shared truth we can only discover together.

### How the three platforms do it

Each platform holds one piece. None is complete alone. Together they produce something new.

#### CivicGraph — what the system actually looks like

587,390 entities. 1.5M relationships. 29.5M records across 254 tables. \$74 billion in government contracts tracked. 301,803 political donations. 30,724 grants indexed.

CivicGraph answers: **Who gets the money? Who makes the decisions? Where are the gaps?**

When a judge scans a postcard QR code and finds no diversion program in their region — that gap is visible because CivicGraph maps what exists and, more importantly, what doesn't. When a funder asks "where should we invest?", CivicGraph shows 873 LGAs identified as funding deserts. When a journalist asks "who benefits from youth detention?", CivicGraph traces the procurement contracts to private operators.

This is the honest signal layer. Not self-reported impact statements. Actual money flows cross-referenced with verified outcomes.

#### JusticeHub — what works and what doesn't

1,775 community models in the Australian Living Map of Alternatives. 128 verified at the top three tiers (Indigenous-led, Effective, Proven). 52,000 justice funding records. 672,000 AusTender contracts.

JusticeHub answers: **What alternatives exist? Where? Run by whom? With what evidence?**

Oonchiumpa's 95% diversion rate isn't a claim — it's a verified entry in the evidence base. The \$1.3M detention cost isn't an estimate — it's from ROGS 2024-25, cross-referenced against actual program costs. When a program says "we work" and the data says otherwise, JusticeHub surfaces the contradiction.

This is the evidence layer. Not advocacy. Not hope. Verified, comparable, searchable evidence about what actually works for young people.

#### Empathy Ledger — who these people actually are

226 storytellers. 5,039 media assets. Consent-governed at the data layer. OCAP principles (Ownership, Control, Access, Possession) as database architecture, not aspiration.

Empathy Ledger answers: **What does the data mean for a real person? What is their actual experience of the system?**

When Nigel says "I feel like I'm panicking" talking to a judge, that is not a data point. It is a sovereign statement from a 14-year-old about what the justice system feels like from inside it. When Laquisha says "Oppression" — one word — that is not a pull quote for a report. It is a diagnosis that no amount of CivicGraph data could produce on its own.

This is the narrative sovereignty layer. Stories owned by the people who lived them. Never extracted. Always governed.

### How they combine in practice

**Scenario 1: The Judges on Country postcard**

A judge holds a card. On the front: Nigel's photo and his words. That is Empathy Ledger. On the back: a QR code. It opens JusticeHub, filtered to the judge's region, showing what programs exist. That is the evidence layer. The data behind those programs — who funds them, how they compare to detention costs, where the gaps are — that is CivicGraph.

One postcard. Three layers. The Third Reality.

**Scenario 2: A grant application for Oonchiumpa**

The application says: "95% diversion rate." JusticeHub provides the verified evidence. CivicGraph shows there are zero comparable programs within 500km — proving the need. Empathy Ledger provides consent-governed stories from Xavier, Laquisha, CB showing what the outcomes look like in human terms. The funder doesn't receive a report. They receive a Third Reality Assessment — data + evidence + story, linked and verifiable.

**Scenario 3: A policy paper on youth detention**

CivicGraph shows: \$1.3M per child per year. 80%+ reoffending. 60%+ Indigenous. 873 LGAs with no funded alternatives. JusticeHub shows: 128 verified programs that work, most unfunded or underfunded. Empathy Ledger shows: what detention actually does to a 16-year-old sent 1,500km from home.

Any one layer alone is dismissible. Together they are undeniable.

### What CivicScope could become

CivicGraph is currently the intelligence engine underneath JusticeHub. But the Civic World Model vision is bigger:

- **Real-time civic intelligence**: not annual reports, but live maps of where money flows, who makes decisions, and what changes
- **Cross-sector application**: the same pattern works for housing, health, disability, environment — any domain where systemic data and human narrative both exist but don't talk to each other
- **Automated policy tracking**: when a state government announces a new youth justice policy, CivicGraph traces whether the money actually follows the announcement
- **Community-controlled verification**: communities use the ALMA tier system to verify whether programs actually work, not just whether they exist
- **Global expansion**: the pattern is not Australia-specific. Diagrama in Spain, JusticeHub International, Maranguka's KPMG-verified model — the architecture works anywhere the honest signal can be captured

### The deeper point

The Third Reality is not a product. It is a bet on a specific theory of change:

**The reason the youth justice system doesn't change is not that people don't care. It is that the people who care are looking at different rooms and drawing different conclusions.**

The judge sees a court file. The community worker sees a young person. The funder sees a budget line. The politician sees a headline. The Elder sees a child who belongs to Country.

They are all looking at the same reality — but they are each seeing only their piece of it.

The Third Reality is what emerges when you force those pieces together. When a judge holds Nigel's photo and scans a QR that shows what programs exist in his region and what they cost compared to detention. When a funder reads a grant application that contains verified outcomes AND the voice of the young person those outcomes describe. When a politician sees a map of funding deserts overlaid with detention rates overlaid with community-led alternatives that work at 97.6% less cost.

That is not data. That is not a story. It is the shared truth that neither could produce alone.

And the bet is: when enough people see it, the system changes. Not because they were told to. Because they can no longer unsee it.

That is what Nigel's postcard does in a judge's hand. That is what the entire ACT ecosystem is built to produce.

pages.excerpt: Nigel, 14
pages.content:
> Nigel, 14

## Context

**Place:** Mparntwe (Alice Springs)
**Voice Owner:** Nigel (N), 14, Double Camp
**Consent Status:** Public

## Story

Nigel is 14 and from Double Camp. He wants to play AFL. He knows what it takes. Go to school. Go consistently. Build the discipline that lets talent become something real.

But between him and that future there is a courtroom.

> "When I'm talking to the judge, I feel like I'm panicking."

A courtroom is designed for adults who understand its language. It is not designed for a 14-year-old from Double Camp who is trying to explain his life in a room full of strangers with authority over his body. The panic is not weakness. It is the correct response to an environment that was never built for him.

Nigel does not need a better lawyer. He needs someone to walk the path with him. Someone who knows that footy training and school attendance and court appearances are not separate problems but the same life, lived by the same kid, in the same week.

That is what [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] does. Not legal representation. Relationship. Fred and the team sit with him in the hard rooms and drive him to the good ones. They hold the whole picture because Nigel's life is not a series of disconnected service referrals. It is one life.

He can see the path to where he wants to go. He just needs someone beside him on it.

## Postcard

"When I'm talking to the judge, I feel like I'm panicking."

pages.title: Why I Started BG Fit
pages.excerpt: Brodie Germaine
pages.content:
> Brodie Germaine

> I started BG Fit because I saw too many of our mob going through the justice system and not getting the support they needed.

## Summary

Brodie shares the founding story of BG Fit — born from witnessing too many Indigenous young people cycling through the justice system without support.

## Story

I started BG Fit because I saw too many of our mob going through the justice system and not getting the support they needed. Growing up in Mount Isa, I saw what happened when young fellas had nothing to do — they'd get into trouble. But when they had sport, when they had something to work towards, everything changed.

I played rugby league at a high level and I know what sport can do for young people. It's not just about fitness — it's about discipline, respect, turning up when you said you would. These are the things that keep our mob strong.

We started with just a gym session on Tuesdays at the PCYC. Five kids turned up the first week. Now we've got 15-20 regulars and the word is spreading. The parents are seeing changes in their kids — better behaviour at school, more confidence, showing up on time.

The goal was never just fitness. It's about creating a pathway. Some of these kids have never had anyone believe in them before. When you show up every week and you're there for them, that means something. That's what BG Fit is about.

pages.title: Wiki Project and Work Sync Contract
pages.excerpt: The wiki is the anchor for what a project or work is. Supabase, Empathy Ledger, and the websites should read from this contract instead of inventing parallel truths.
pages.content:
> The wiki is the anchor for what a project or work **is**. Supabase, Empathy Ledger, and the websites should read from this contract instead of inventing parallel truths.

## Why This Exists

The ACT system now has enough moving parts that identity drift becomes expensive fast:

- Tractorpedia holds the durable memory
- Empathy Ledger holds the live editorial, story, photo, and video layer
- Supabase holds operational rows, sync state, and history
- the websites compose the public surface

If those layers all define project identity independently, the same thing ends up with three names, two slugs, and the wrong photos.

This contract fixes that.

## Knowledge-Base Method

This follows the [[llm-knowledge-base|LLM Knowledge Base]] pattern and should continue to.

### The layers stay distinct

| Layer | Purpose | What belongs there |
|---|---|---|
| `wiki/raw/` | Immutable source memory | transcripts, articles, screenshots, datasets, exports |
| `wiki/sources/` | One-summary-per-source bridge | what a raw source contains, who/what it touches |
| `wiki/projects/`, `wiki/art/`, etc. | Durable entity / concept memory | projects, works, communities, methods, decisions |
| `wiki/synthesis/` | Compounding answers | query outputs worth keeping |
| Empathy Ledger | Live editorial and consented proof | stories, storytellers, galleries, photos, video, hero selections |
| Supabase | Operational mirror and sync state | `projects`, sync metadata, history tables, CRM/finance joins |
| Websites | Public composition | curated pages, routing, enquiry, syndication |

The wiki should remain the place where ACT's understanding compounds. It should not become a media bucket or a redundant content store.

The same applies to people. `wiki/people/` is a curated explanatory layer, not a mirror of every EL storyteller or every operational contact. The curation rule lives in [[people/README|People Index]].

## The Rule

For any real ACT project or work:

1. **Name it and frame it in the wiki**
2. **Classify it through the identity rules**
3. **Link live stories/media in Empathy Ledger**
4. **Mirror canonical identifiers into Supabase**
5. **Compose it on the website from generated snapshots**

That means the website is downstream of the wiki, not parallel to it.

## Canonical Fields

Every load-bearing page that might sync to the website, Empathy Ledger, or Supabase should have frontmatter like this.

### Required for operational/project surfaces

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `title` | Human-readable canonical title |
| `status` | Current lifecycle state (`Active`, `Paused`, `Ideation`, etc.) |
| `date` | Last structural update date for the page |
| `entity_type` | What kind of object this page is |
| `tagging_mode` | How it behaves across systems |
| `canonical_slug` | Canonical slug across wiki/site/EL |
| `canonical_code` | Canonical cross-system project code |

### Strongly recommended for website / EL composition

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `website_slug` | Website-facing slug if different from wiki file slug |
| `website_path` | Primary ACT-site route for the page |
| `public_surface` | `project`, `hub`, `work`, or `index` |
| `cluster` | Cluster or field this page belongs to |
| `parent_project` | Canonical parent slug when this is a work, sub-project, or cluster member |
| `empathy_ledger_key` | Canonical EL project key when it differs from `canonical_slug` |

### Current controlled value sets

- `entity_type`
  - `project`
  - `project-hub`
  - `cluster-hub`
  - `sub-project`
  - `deliverable`
  - `work`
  - `work-series`
  - `work-placeholder`
  - `methodology`
  - `flagship-program`
  - `pitch-package`
  - `working-draft`
  - `partner-proof`
  - `alias-brand`
  - `community-strategy`
  - `method-lab`

- `tagging_mode`
  - `own-code`
  - `parent-code`
  - `alias-of`
  - `related-proof`
  - `no-tag-yet`

- `public_surface`
  - `project`
  - `hub`
  - `work`
  - `index`

## Example: Project

```yaml
---
title: JusticeHub
status: Active
date: 2026-04-11
entity_type: project-hub
tagging_mode: own-code
canonical_slug: justicehub
canonical_code: ACT-JH
website_slug: justicehub
website_path: /justicehub
public_surface: project
cluster: justicehub
empathy_ledger_key: justicehub
---
```

## Example: Work

```yaml
---
title: Gold.Phone
status: Active
date: 2026-04-11
entity_type: work
tagging_mode: own-code
canonical_slug: gold-phone
canonical_code: ACT-GP
website_slug: gold-phone
website_path: /projects/gold-phone
public_surface: work
cluster: act-studio
parent_project: act-studio
empathy_ledger_key: gold-phone
---
```

## What Syncs Where

### To the website

The ACT site should consume generated wiki snapshots, not scrape page bodies ad hoc forever. The project snapshot should at minimum expose:

- `slug`
- `title`
- `summary`
- `overview`
- `status`
- `code`
- `canonicalSlug`
- `canonicalCode`
- `entityType`
- `taggingMode`
- `cluster`
- `parentProject`
- `websiteSlug`
- `websitePath`
- `projectPagePath`
- `publicSurface`
- `empathyLedgerKey`

For the five flagship ACT public fields, the system should also emit a dedicated pack snapshot:

- `wiki/output/flagship-project-packs.json` in the wiki repo
- `src/data/wiki-flagship-project-packs.generated.json` in the ACT website repo

Those packs are the direct handoff for richer public composition and EL alignment. They should carry:

- the canonical identity fields above
- the flagship page summary / overview / system position
- curated key people
- key source bridges
- website path + EL key in one object

That gives the website and Empathy Ledger a stable object to consume without reparsing long-form wiki markdown every time.

### To Supabase

Supabase should mirror canonical identity, not redefine it.

Current practical rule:

- `public.projects` should carry the canonical code
- `public.projects.metadata.canonical_slug` should carry the canonical wiki slug
- wrapper or legacy rows should point back to the canonical slug/code, not diverge from it

Supabase is the operational mirror and history surface. It is not the place where project identity is invented.

### To Empathy Ledger

Empathy Ledger should use the canonical slug or explicit `empathy_ledger_key` to attach:

- hero image / hero video
- galleries
- storyteller portraits
- featured stories
- syndicated articles

That keeps media and stories attached to the same identity the wiki defines.

## Ongoing History

The system's history should remain legible across layers:

- **Wiki history** — durable page evolution, decisions, synthesis, backlinks
- **`wiki/log.md`** — operational trail of wiki maintenance actions
- **Supabase history** — operational rows, sync metadata, CRM / finance / opportunity traces
- **Empathy Ledger history** — stories, media, editorial manifests, consent-aware live proof

The website should present the current composed view, but it should not be the only place where history can be understood.

## Works and Art

The `wiki/art/` directory should remain the **conceptual and curatorial layer**.

That means:
- `wiki/art/art-projects.md` is the studio-line index
- individual load-bearing works can still live in `wiki/projects/` when they behave like real projects or operational works
- the website's `Works` layer should compose those wiki pages with EL photos/video/story fragments

Do **not** duplicate the same work article across `wiki/art/` and `wiki/projects/`. The index can point. The canonical page should stay singular.

## Retagging Rule

Reclassification is allowed and expected.

When a page changes shape:

1. update the page frontmatter
2. update [[project-identity-and-tagging-system|Project Identity and Tagging System]] if the classification changed
3. rerun the sync chain
4. let Supabase / EL / site converge from that updated contract

That is how the system grows without freezing mistakes in place.

pages.title: Workshops at BCV
pages.excerpt: A rolling program of short-form workshops on Country — land practice, making, writing, systems. Hands in the soil by morning, a real conversation by afternoon. Come for one, come for a series.
pages.content:
> A rolling program of short-form workshops on Country — land practice, making, writing, systems. Hands in the soil by morning, a real conversation by afternoon. Come for one, come for a series.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FM-EXP-workshops-at-bcv | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## What it is

We run workshops at [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] as the everyday way people drop into ACT's practice. Half-day and full-day sessions, usually open to public enrolment, priced to be reachable. Some are taught by ACT staff, some by visiting practitioners, some in partnership with [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] across the two sites.

The workshops are how we keep a porous edge to the farm — places where people who aren't yet in a residency, retreat, or cohort program can still meet the land practice and the method.

## Who it's for

- Locals from Witta, Maleny, and the Sunshine Coast hinterland
- Makers, writers, practitioners looking for short-form land time
- Community groups running single-day offsites
- People thinking about a longer engagement (residency, cohort, retreat) who want to try the gate first

## What happens

Content varies. A running program includes:

- **Land practice** — regenerative ag, native planting, weed management, water systems
- **Making** — pottery, food preserving, textile practice, material work in partnership with [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]]
- **Writing and story** — story craft sessions, [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] method intros
- **Systems and facilitation** — short sessions for people who want to learn how we hold rooms

Workshops typically run 3–6 hours with a shared meal. Some are single sessions; others are 3–6 week series.

## Price, duration, capacity

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Duration** | Half-day, full-day, or multi-session series |
| **Capacity** | 6–20 per workshop |
| **Price** | Per-workshop ticketed, priced for accessibility. Concession places held on most sessions |
| **Includes** | Teaching, materials (workshop-dependent), shared meal |
| **Season** | Year-round; some seasonal (harvest, planting) |

## Ecosystem links

- [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] — Witta side of the workshop program; see [[experiences/harvest-pairings|Harvest Pairings]] for paired series
- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — material practice workshops
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — storytelling workshop lineage
- [[act-farm|ACT Farm]] — the hosting program
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]]

## Related case studies

- <Placeholder — workshop case studies written as series complete>

## How to inquire

Individual workshops are ticketed — the current calendar is on the ACT Farm site at `/experiences/workshops-at-bcv`. For custom workshops for a group or organisation, inquire via the same page.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], Workshops at BCV are the porous-edge version of the method — half-day and full-day sessions where people who aren't yet in a residency, retreat, or cohort can still meet the land practice. Here's how the four phases show up across a typical workshop:

- **Listen** — orientation to the land and the day; teachers introducing themselves through what they make
- **Curiosity** — short inputs followed by working time; the kind of question that only surfaces once your hands are doing something
- **Action** — land practice, making, writing, or systems work — depending on the workshop; a shared meal with the cohort
- **Art** — what the participant takes home (the pot, the jar, the sentence, the practice); a frame for why the workshop work connects to the wider [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]]

Workshops are how ACT keeps a porous edge to the farm — places where you can try the gate before you decide whether to walk through it.
